newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU open to bigger Europol crimefighting role.
newsitem.headline: EU open to bigger Europol crimefighting role.

text.p: The European Union said on Monday it was prepared to strengthen the powers of its Europol police agency so it could more effectively combat organised crime running rampant across its free borders.

EU interior ministers made the proposal when endorsing a report of more than 40 pages from a select group of the 15-nation bloc's top policemen, magistrates and interior officials which painted a grim picture of a grouping out of its depth in crime.

Laxer border controls, EU rules allowing people, goods and money to move unfettered and lush EU subsidies have, the report said, created a playground for stication, including use of the Internet, far outstrips that of crime fighters.
"Crime is more and more organised and uses to its advantage the free circulation of goods, capital, services and people, as well as technological innovation," the ministers said.

Among the ideas to be put to the EU's Amsterdam Summit on June 16-17 will be "the enhancement of the role of Europol", approximation of criminal legislation in areas such as incrimination and bringing judicial cooperation to a level comparable to police cooperation.

At the moment the Hague-based EU agency is limited to exchanging information between the different national police forces, and only once the 14 EU member states who have not yet done so have ratified the convention making it fully operational will it be able to pool and analyse the data.
As a result of the thinking under way, Europol would in a new stage become more "operative" and make suggestions and coordinate with national crime fighters.

"This would mean that Europol might, for instance, be involved in assisting police teams in member states...by providing expertise," Dutch Justice Minister Winnie Sorgdrager told a news conference after ministers met.

The plan falls well short of the European-style U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) demanded by Germany, where Eurocops could initiate their own investigations, carry out raids and arrest suspects.
But what was agreed was well beyond what was acceptable to some member states several weeks ago.
"Even the member states who were most reticent have decided to support this," German Secretary of State for the Interior Kurt Schelter told reporters.
Britain, in particular, was careful to avoid any wording which might give rise to suspicions of EU-level interference in its police and legal process.
The EU's Justice Commissioner Anita Gradin said that EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam in June needed to enshrine a stronger legal basis for combatting organised crime. 281735 GMT apr 97
